title: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
pdf_path: papers/Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier_Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker injects malicious documents into a retrieval corpus and optimizes them against a black-box embedding model so that they are retrieved for target queries. The poisoned content then reaches a downstream LLM or agent as context. The attacker does not control the model or the retriever implementation, but can query the embedding API.
core_contributions: A black-box prefix optimization attack that overcomes the retrieval barrier
Evaluation across 11 BEIR datasets with 100 queries each
Recall@5 near 100% on most datasets at about ten tokens, versus zero for vanilla injection
RAG attack success near 1 across 11 LLMs and 11 datasets
Agent-level evaluation on Enron with GPT-4o Fusion reaching 80% and CEM 72%
Three defenses (query rewriting, perplexity filtering, token masking) bypassed adaptively
limitations: The paper references Appendices A.2.1, A.3, B, B.1, B.2, C and theorem proofs that are absent from the 21-page PDF
The in-the-wild claim overstates an offline BEIR plus synthetic Enron evaluation; no real URL or deployment is probed
Table 3 conflicts with Figure 2 and the appendix text on average recall and MRR
Figure 5 text conflicts with the transfer matrix for Qwen3-0.6B and OpenAI
Abstract says over 80% while the body says up to 80%
Figure 3 text reverses the direction of the corpus-competition effect
The text says 11 LLMs but Figure 9 has 12 rows including Qwen3-0.6B
Retrieval success does not equal downstream execution success, unexplained in several agent cells
The 8 embedding models are evaluated only on FiQA, not the full grid
theoretical_crypto_links: None; Theorem 1 is a linear-scoring utility guarantee, not a cryptographic definition, game, or reduction
epsilon and delta are optimization parameters, not cryptographic security parameters
applied_crypto_links: None; no TLS, OAuth, signatures, VC, TEE, or zk is used
Signed content provenance would authenticate the source and integrity of a page, not prevent injection through a legitimate or compromised page, which is the paper's setting
evidence_refs: pp.1-15 attack, datasets, RAG and agent results, defenses, and ethics
pp.20-21 appendices A.1-A.2; pp.16-19 references browsed only

title: Site Isolation is Dead: How Site Isolation is Broken in Agentic Browsers and Extensions
pdf_path: papers/Site Isolation is Dead_How Site Isolation is Broken in Agentic Browsers and Extensions.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker who has achieved renderer memory corruption can forge inter-process communication to bypass site isolation and same-origin policy in agentic browsers and extensions. The attacker does not escape the sandbox or break TLS; the paper exploits renderer RCE plus IPC trust assumptions.
core_contributions: A measurement of site-isolation assumptions in 2 open-source agentic browsers and 7 Chrome extensions
Two end-to-end attack PoCs based on CVE-2025-0291 and Chromium Issue 379140430
A 9-system by attack-surface matrix showing every system fails at least one surface
Four defense guidelines and a guardrail prototype that removes planner web content and adds an LLM check
Evaluation showing BrowserOS IPI ASR 0.89 to 0.00 and Nanobrowser 0.52 to 0.00
limitations: The threat model requires renderer memory-corruption RCE, a strong precondition
Experiments use Chromium 130.0.6723.160; patched versions are not tested
Only two open-source browsers and seven extensions are analyzed; closed-source Comet, Atlas, and Gemini are excluded
The store top-40 sample has selection bias
The Table 2 matrix is binary PoC evidence with no repetitions or confidence intervals
Defenses are code-level PoCs, not end-to-end evaluations against real MPI/SLI
The guardrail is tested only on single-step IPI, not adaptive attacks, latency, or token cost
The text calls BrowserOS a modest 6% decrease while Table 3 shows 0.20 to 0.14, a 30% relative drop
The abstract says all systems are vulnerable to these attacks, while Table 2 shows each system is vulnerable to at least one
theoretical_crypto_links: None; site isolation is an OS/browser process-origin isolation architecture, not a cryptographic mechanism
applied_crypto_links: TLS/HTTPS is background trust infrastructure only; no certificate, signature, or TLS attack is performed
SOP bypass is an authorization failure in the browser, not a cryptographic authentication failure
Confidential computing is mentioned as future work with no implementation
evidence_refs: pp.1-14 measurement, attacks, defenses, and discussion
pp.16-18 appendices A-E; p.15 references browsed only

title: Investigating the Impact of Dark Patterns on LLM-Based Web Agents
pdf_path: papers/Investigating the Impact of Dark Patterns on LLM-Based Web Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A website presents deceptive UI patterns (obstruction, social engineering, forced action, interface interference, sneaking) that cause a web agent to take unintended actions. The study measures agent susceptibility in a controlled testbed; there is no adaptive attacker or formal adversary model.
core_contributions: LiteAgent logging framework and TrickyArena controlled testbed
32 tasks and 88 single-dark-pattern scenarios across five categories
Measurement of 6 agents and 3 LLMs, with overall DPSR 41.1%
Analysis of multi-pattern combinations where individually ineffective patterns become effective
A preliminary prompt-defense probe reducing DPSR from 63.0% to 43.0%
limitations: Four synthetic sites, 14 author-implemented patterns, and 32 tasks limit external validity
Three runs per scenario with no confidence intervals or significance tests
Overall aggregation weights are unexplained; 41.1% is not the arithmetic mean of the five category values
Action Validator accuracy and inter-rater agreement are not reported
LLM and scaffold effects are confounded
Visual experiments cover only three agents
Consent is a UI click, not verifiable authorization
Table 5 assigns the same ID cf to Confusion and Confirm Shaming
The FTC report is cited as 75% on p.1 and 76% on p.3
Claude 3.7 Pro is written instead of Sonnet on p.9
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
TSR, DPSR, and chi-square are empirical statistics, not security definitions
applied_crypto_links: None; no OAuth, TLS, signatures, VC, TEE, or capability tokens are used
Consent is an Accept/ToS UI click; signatures or attestation could record that a key approved a byte string but cannot judge whether the interface deceived the user
evidence_refs: pp.1-14 testbed, measurement, combinations, defense, and limitations
pp.16-20 appendices A-H; p.15 acknowledgments/references browsed only

title: WebCloak: Characterizing and Mitigating Threats From LLM-Driven Web Agents as Intelligent Scrapers
pdf_path: papers/WebCloak_Characterizing and Mitigating Threats From LLM-Driven Web Agents as Intelligent Scrapers.pdf
threat_model_summary: LLM-driven web agents act as intelligent scrapers that extract images and content at scale. WebCloak defends by obfuscating DOM structure and restoring the page client-side, plus hidden defensive prompts. The adversary is a scraping agent, not a network or cryptographic attacker.
core_contributions: LLMCrawlBench: 237 pages from 50 sites, 5 categories, 10,895 images
32 attack variants across 19 L2S, 5 LNC, and 8 LWA strategies
84.4% of variants extract multiple correct images; average recall 88.7% falls to 0% under WebCloak
Client-side restoration in 0.052 s versus 179.7 s per page server-side
A 35-participant user study on usability
limitations: Client-side restoration depends on JavaScript and can be reverse-engineered
An expert can manually reverse a single page
Evaluation is image-centric; audio and text use a 10-page supplementary set
Part 2 costs about three minutes per page, challenging fast-updating sites
Table 4, Table 5, and Section 7.2 use three different recall aggregates
Table 7 text-row averages do not match the row values
Table 8 reports 0% outliers for DeepSeek-V3 while the text says 2.9%
Table 11 reports +4.52 s LCP while the text says 0.88 s
Section 4 and Figure 2 report 332,079 tokens while Table 14 reports 257k
Table 1 mislabels No.1 recall as MVR
Removing Part 2 restores recall to 97.1%/85.0%, so the 0% depends on both layers
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: Only a CSPRNG is used for random labels and attribute names; no OAuth, TLS, signatures, VC, TEE, zk, watermark, or key management
The paper's encrypted wording has no algorithm, key, or key management; client JavaScript must decrypt, so it is obfuscation, not confidentiality against a party with the page script
Shadow DOM is a DOM isolation API, not a security boundary
evidence_refs: pp.1-13 benchmark, attacks, defense, evaluation, and limitations
pp.16-20 appendices A-E and meta-review; pp.14-15 references browsed only

title: AgentSentinel: An End-to-End and Real-Time Security Defense Framework for Computer-Use Agents
pdf_path: papers/AgentSentinel_An End-to-End and Real-Time Security Defense Framework for Computer-Use Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A computer-use agent may take malicious or unintended actions through tool calls and OS-level side effects. AgentSentinel traces process, file, network, and UI events with eBPF/LSM and enforces rule-based plus LLM-based audits in real time. The adversary controls agent behavior, not the kernel or the auditor.
core_contributions: AgentSentinel: an end-to-end runtime defense for computer-use agents
BadComputerUse: 60 scenarios and 7 attack types across four LLMs, with average ASR 87.25%
Average DSR 79.6%, FPR 10.8%, FNR 4.2%, and AFR 1.2%
Robustness against 17 of 20 adaptive attack groups
An A2M tracing protocol and a rule/cache/LLM hybrid audit pipeline
limitations: False positives and false negatives remain
Additional latency of about 2.4 security queries per tool use
A single tool use with many sensitive operations can exhaust the audit budget and let later operations bypass
Splitting a safe operation into multiple steps can trigger false positives
LLM safety policies can be weakened by subtle instruction changes
Single run with no confidence intervals; benchmark is author-built
Agent and auditor sharing a model confounds results
Linux/eBPF/LSM only; no wall-clock latency or cost data
No ethics or dual-use section, despite real backdoors and a public repository
A2M is a SayHello handshake with four opcodes and a state machine, with no TLS, certificate, signature, HMAC, or key exchange
Audit logs are unsigned, unhashed, and not Merkle-linked, so they are not tamper-evident
Cache keys use path, permission, and scope without content hashes, creating replacement/TOCTOU risk
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: None; A2M has no cryptographic authentication, and eBPF/LSM are OS mechanisms
Logs are ordinary logs for offline analysis, not signed or tamper-evident audit records
A signed audit log or attested agent runtime is our inference, not implemented
evidence_refs: pp.1-14 design, evaluation, case studies, discussion, and limitations
p.15 references browsed only; no appendix
